results.title: HiFloat4 Format for End-To-End Reinforcement Learning Post-Training of Large Language Models
results.content:
To remove this overhead while preserving the accuracy gain,
we propose Rollout Residual Quantization (Rollout-ResQ),
which augments the standard FP4 rollout computation with a residual correction term
constrained to a hardware-friendly sparsity pattern .
The two ingredients are inseparable:
the residual, inspired by the decomposition of ,
captures the outlier-driven error that vanilla FP4 rollouts incur,
while the imposed sparsity ensures the correction itself
runs at a small fraction of a dense FP4 GEMM.
The result is a single, lightweight correction added to the FP4 rollout path—
preserving accuracy close to the higher-precision-activation alternatives
while retaining true FP4 GEMM throughput end-to-end.
Our contributions are as follows: [...] a single residual correction term constrained to a hardware-friendly sparsity pattern,
added only to the FP4 rollout matmul — a lightweight correction
that recovers most of the precision lost to outlier-driven underflow
without inflating the rollout’s compute footprint.
On Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Rollout-ResQ paired with the HiFloat4 (HiF4) format —
whose three-level hierarchical scaling preserves resolution under FP4’s tight 4-bit budget —
closes the accuracy gap to BF16 from 4.9%4.9\% to 1.1%1.1\%,
bringing fully quantized FP4 RL within striking distance of full precision.
Applied to the open-standard MXFP4, the same recipe narrows the gap from 13.6%13.6\% to 5.3%5.3\%, revealing that FP4 format choice is a key factor that determines the ceiling on recoverable accuracy. [...] Together, these results establish HiF4 as the enabling format
for end-to-end FP4 RL post-training,
and Rollout-ResQ as the activation-side mechanism that makes the gap to BF16 closable.

results.title: Aligning Training and Rollout Policies for End-to-End FP4 RL on Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
results.content:
Guided by this finding, we propose MoeResQ, which adapts RolloutResQ to align the training and rollout sides by applying a residual correction on the training side as well. We further study a fine-grained configuration that quantizes the linear layers of the experts only. Together, these choices close the training-inference alignment as well as the accuracy gap to full precision (BF16) for FP4 RL on MoE models. [...] Prior work has explored low-precision computation for RL, with 8-bit formats on the rollout side, and Li et al. (2026) on both the training and rollout policies Xi et al. (2026). Most recently, QeRLHuang et al. (2026) applied weight-only quantization to the rollout policy in combination with LoRA Hu et al. (2021), keeping activations and gradients in higher precision, while RolloutResQ Mak et al. (2026) introduced a residual correction for the rollout activations and quantized both the training and rollout sides to 4-bit. A central challenge shared by these methods is the mismatch between the training and rollout sides, which has so far been studied only for dense models Yao et al. (2025). [...] Base on the above analysis, we present MoeResQ, an symmetric recipe for recovering the precision loss induced by the training–inference mismatch in MoE models under fully FP4 RL.
Having identified that applying quantization recovery to only one side—training or inference—is the principal failure mode,
MoeResQ applies RC to the same layers on both training and inference, maximizing the symmetry between the two policies and thereby minimizing the mismatch.
Concretely, during rollout we apply the activation correction of Equation 1. During training, the forward pass uses the same residual correction as the inference side (Equation 1).

[...] We present, to our knowledge, the first end-to-end FP4 RL post-training, in which both the rollout and training policies, including their forward and backward passes, operate at 4-bit precision. A systematic study reveals that the dominant source of degradation in FP4 RL is not training-side quantization error but rollout activation quantization: outliers stretch the dynamic range so far that a large number of activation values underflow to zero under FP4. Counterintuitively, restoring the training policy to higher precision while keeping the rollout in FP4 makes accuracy worse than full FP4 baseline, exposing rollout-training mismatch as the principal failure mode and ruling out standard pretraining-style fixes.
